cues.text: Okay. Pick up your phone. Remember this little box? Allow this app to track your activity?
You probably tapped, Ask App Not to Track, without even thinking.
Millions of people did the same thing. And Meta, the company behind Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp, says that one tap would cost it around ten billion dollars.
I'm Vio. This is the story of how one button started a war between two of the richest companies on Earth.
And how Mark Zuckerberg is now trying to win it with an AI that shops for you.
First, you need to understand one thing. Meta owns the apps. But it doesn't own the phones.
Almost every Instagram scroll and every WhatsApp message happens on a phone made by Apple, or running Google's software.
So Meta is like a shop that pays rent in somebody else's building.
It's a huge, very rich shop. But the landlord still makes the rules.
And for years, Apple had been telling everyone that it was the privacy company. It even put up a giant billboard in Las Vegas saying, what happens on your iPhone, stays on your iPhone.
And Meta's business runs on ads. Really good ads. Ads that seem to know you.
Say you look at a pair of sneakers in a shopping app. Ten minutes later, those exact sneakers show up on Instagram.
That works because your iPhone had a hidden ID number. Apps could use it to follow you from one app to another, and tell Meta what you did.
It had a very boring name. The I D F A. The identifier for advertisers. But it was worth a fortune.
Think of it as a little spy, quietly following you everywhere you go on your phone. And advertisers paid a lot for what that spy saw.
And here's the thing. Most people had no idea the spy was there.
Then, in April 2021, Apple released iOS fourteen point five.
Now every app had to ask first. Do you want this app to track you, yes or no?
Meta saw it coming. Months earlier, it bought full-page ads in big American newspapers, saying, we're standing up to Apple for small businesses everywhere.
Apple's answer was simple. It said this was about standing up for its users.
Imagine your landlord putting a big sign on your shop door, asking every customer, do you want this shop to watch what you do? Most people are going to say no.
And the users chose. In the first weeks, one analytics company estimated that only around four to six percent of iPhone users in the US said yes.
Meta's ads got less precise. Advertisers couldn't see as clearly what was working, so they spent less.
In February 2022, Meta told its investors the Apple change would cost it about ten billion dollars that year. Its own finance chief called that number a best guess.
The next day, Meta's stock fell about twenty six percent.
Roughly two hundred and thirty billion dollars in value disappeared in a single day. At the time, the biggest one-day drop for any American company in history.
One button. Ten billion dollars a year. That's about twenty seven million dollars, every single day.
So Zuckerberg needed a way out of the landlord's building.
First, he bet on the metaverse. Then the AI race exploded, and Meta was suddenly chasing companies like OpenAI and Google.
Meta built its own AI models and gave many of them away for free. But for a while, rivals kept pulling ahead.
So Meta started spending like crazy. Billions on a new superintelligence team, and, reportedly, pay packages for top AI researchers that sounded like football transfer fees.
And in September 2026, Meta showed what all that money was for. An AI agent called Muse.
Muse doesn't just chat. It does things. You can ask it to plan a trip, send an email, or buy you something.
Meta says it can check out from stores like Walmart, Best Buy and Sephora, and it lives right inside WhatsApp.
It's free to start, with paid plans at twenty and a hundred dollars a month. For now, it's only available in the United States.
Now think about what that means. If you tell Muse what you want, there's no need for a spy to follow you around. You just told it yourself.
And because it all happens inside Meta's own apps, Apple's little box never even pops up.
And at its big event, Zuckerberg even described a possible future where Muse takes a small cut of the things it buys for you. So Meta could earn from the ad, and from the sale.
Meta is also bringing Muse to its smart glasses. Picture this. You see a jacket on the street, you ask your glasses about it, and a few seconds later, it's on its way to you.
That's either the coolest thing ever, or the creepiest. Maybe both.
And remember, Muse can make mistakes. And reportedly, Meta's own terms limit what it pays back if the agent buys something you didn't want.
So here's my question. Would you let Meta's AI spend your money? Tell me in the comments.
And subscribe. Next time, there's another tech war you didn't know was happening.
Apple took away the button. Now Meta wants to become the button.
